sections.report:
Walk (working notes), The whole piece:
1. Purpose clear in one sentence: yes
2. Image and headline make one idea: yes (there's no image; the headline alone carries it)
3. Every element does a job: yes
4. One mood and era: yes
5. Copy finished: yes
6. Same kind of element looks the same: yes
7. Mood fits the message: yes
8. Heading names its section: yes

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open in step 5. The image is 1280×800 (one screen), so I worked from the whole image.

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

One finding has no checklist line (copy read as a stranger would). I'm passing it to the director:
1. *(Off-checklist, copy)* **The times and the date are vague where passengers will act on them.** In the first paragraph (about x 120–775, y 150–230), "every forty minutes between early morning and late evening" gives no first or last sailing. In the note at y ≈ 372, "Timetables change in winter" doesn't say when winter starts or what changes. A passenger planning the last crossing home can't tell whether 21:00 is "late evening". Someone travelling in November can't tell whether the times above still apply. The note sends them to a noticeboard at the landing, which they only see once they've already arrived. Times and dates are what readers act on and later hold the operator to, so a line that can be read two ways is a defect here, not a style note. Fix: give the first and last departure times. Give the date range for the winter timetable, or say where to check it before leaving home. Defect. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- The headline says exactly what the page holds and who it's for ("Notes for ferry passengers"), so a stranger knows the subject and audience in one glance.
- The piece is one quiet, consistent whole. It uses one sans family, one dark headline over grey text, and no ornaments, boxes or rules. Nothing distracts from the information. That calm, neutral tone suits plain service information.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes

sections.report:
**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** No.
   - **Where:** the two body paragraphs (x≈120–776, y≈150–335) look about 19 px. The closing note, "Timetables change in winter. Check the noticeboard at the landing before you travel." (y≈362–382), looks about 16 px. Both are the same pale blue-grey and the same regular weight.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** the only difference between the two is about 3 px of size. So the note doesn't read as its own level, like a caption or an aside. It reads as a third paragraph that came out slightly smaller by accident. It also sits lowest on the page, and it is the one line that asks the reader to do something before they travel. A reader skimming past the paragraphs is likely to skip it.
   - **Why:** sizes only a few points apart don't read as separate levels. They look like mistakes (Bringhurst). Smaller differences should come from weight or colour, not from another size (Wathan and Schoger, *Refactoring UI*: "bolder, not bigger; lighter, not smaller"). Each level should be easy to tell from the next at a glance (Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*).
   - **Fix:** decide what the note is. If it's a warning to act on, which fits this page, set it at body size and separate it by weight, colour or a label (for example a bold "Winter timetables"), so it stands out from the paragraphs instead of fading below them. If it really is a footnote, make it clearly smaller, well under body size. Either way, drop the 19-vs-16 near-match.
   - **Type:** defect (the action line gets lost) and convention (sizes from a scale).
   - **Weight:** major. This is the line most likely to stop someone making a wasted trip.

**What's working.**
- **The title clearly comes first.** "Notes for ferry passengers" is set at about 40 px, bold and near-black, against pale regular body text. The eye has no doubt where to start, and it learns at once what the page is about.
- **The title differs from the body in more than size.** Weight and value change together with size, so the step from title to body reads at a glance and not only by measuring.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (text levels distinct, no two sizes almost the same).

sections.report:
**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** All the content is in one block in the top-left: roughly x 120–780, y 80–385 on a frame about 1280×800. The only dark element is the headline, and it sits at the top-left corner. Nothing on the right or in the bottom half balances it. About 60% of the frame is empty. That space is gathered, which is good, but it reads as leftover. The page looks unfinished, as if content failed to load, rather than calm. This follows Arnheim (*Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance"): a heavy side needs a counterweight, and isolation and position change weight. A left-aligned text column with open space to the right is a normal web default, and reading is not harder for it, so this is mainly about how finished the page looks. Two ways to fix it:
   - Give the empty area a job. The winter-timetable note is the one line passengers need to act on, and it could sit in the right column as a counterweight.
   - Or set the column on a deliberate margin system, for example a centred measure with the block lowered, so the space looks chosen.

   Taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- Everything shares one left edge at x≈120 with no near-misses. The single column reads as one grid, and the eye runs straight down it without hunting.
- The gaps are steady and about one line deep: headline to body, between paragraphs, and before the note. Together with a short line length, this makes the copy read as one calm, continuous notice.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (visual weight balances).

sections.report:
The Text section applies, and one of its 30 lines fails: all the copy below the heading is pale grey and too faint to read comfortably. The other 29 lines pass.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does text on a plain background reach 4.5:1 contrast (3:1 for large text), placeholder and helper text included?** No.
   - **Where:** both body paragraphs (x ≈ 120–776, y ≈ 150–335, about 19 px) and the winter note (y ≈ 362–382, about 15–16 px). All of it is a light grey that looks close to #9CA3AF, on white. That looks like about 2.5:1, the worst end of the range in the reference entry. This is an estimate by eye; take the real colour with a picker to confirm.
   - **What the viewer meets:** only the near-black heading reads at a glance. The ferry's service details look disabled or faded, like placeholder text. On a phone outdoors at a landing, or for older passengers, they will be hard to read.
   - **The note is the worst case.** "Timetables change in winter. Check the noticeboard at the landing before you travel." is the one line a passenger has to act on, and it is the smallest and faintest text on the page. A reader skimming past it can miss the winter change and turn up for a ferry that isn't running.
   - **Why:** WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) asks for 4.5:1. At 19 px regular the body does not count as large text, so the 3:1 allowance does not apply.
   - **Fix direction:** darken the text until it reaches at least 4.5:1 on white, for example a mid-to-dark slate like #4B5563. The heading can still stand out by weight and size rather than by washing out the body. Do not make the winter note fainter than the body; give it at least the body's contrast, or more emphasis.
   - **Type and weight:** defect, convention (WCAG). Major.

**What's working.**
- **The measure and spacing suit reading.** Paragraph lines run about 72–76 characters, and the line spacing (about 1.5) and the space between paragraphs keep the three short blocks distinct without drifting apart.
- **The type scale is clean.** A bold heading at about 40 px, one body size and one small note size: three levels with clear steps, all in one sans family (it looks like Inter).

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (text on a plain background reaches 4.5:1 contrast).

**Section.** Color: applies. The piece is near-black and one cool gray on white, with no accent and no status colors.

**Findings**
None.

The body copy is a defect, but it belongs to the Text section. All three paragraphs (x≈120–775, y≈150–385) are set in a pale cool gray that looks like about #9CA3AF on white, roughly 2.5:1. That is below WCAG 1.4.3's 4.5:1 for normal text. It also makes the actual ferry information look disabled or like placeholder text. The 13–14 px winter-timetable note at y≈372 is the worst of the three, and it is also the line passengers most need to act on. The fix is to set the body in a dark gray of at least 4.5:1, roughly #4B5563 or darker, and use size and weight rather than paleness to separate the note. I didn't count this under any color line, because the checklist puts each defect under one line only.

**What's working.**
- The palette is very small: one dark neutral for the headline and one gray for the copy, on white. There is nothing to clash and nothing that pulls the eye away from the headline, which suits a plain notice.
- The page passes the grayscale test. The headline is the only dark mass, so it stays the clear entry point when the color is removed.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure
